title: The Treasure Map
summary: A boy and his cousin follow an old hand-drawn map from their grandfather's attic to a hidden family chest in the hills.
poll: Old family objects are more interesting than new things you can buy in a store.

versions.title: The Treasure Map
versions.text:
Faisal likes his grandpa. They clean the attic.

Noura finds a chest. She opens it. Inside is an old map!

The map is brown. It shows a hill. There is an X mark.

What is this X? Grandpa looks at it. My dad made this map, he says. He hid something near the hill.

The next day, they walk up the hill. They see three rocks. Then they see a tree.

They dig by the tree. They dig and dig. Faisal feels something hard.

It is a small chest! They open it. Inside is a compass, a photo, and a note.

The note is old. Their great-grandpa wrote it. He hid it as a kid.

They run home with the chest. Grandpa is glad. He tells them tales.

versions.title: The Treasure Map
versions.text:
Faisal visits his grandfather every Friday. One day, they clean the attic.

Noura opens an old box. Inside, she finds a folded map. The map is brown and old.

It shows their house and a hill. Near the hill, there is a mark. It looks like an X.

What does this X mean? asks Faisal. Grandfather looks at the map. My father drew this long ago, he says. I think he hid something near that hill.

The next day, the cousins walk to the hill. They follow the map. They see three big rocks. Then they see one old tree.

Near the tree, they start to dig. They dig for a while. Then Faisal feels something hard. It is a small chest!

Inside the chest, they find an old compass, a photo, and a letter. Their great-grandfather wrote the letter. He hid the chest when he was a boy.

Faisal and Noura carry the chest home. Grandfather is very surprised. Then he tells them stories about his father.

versions.title: The Treasure Map
versions.text:
Every Friday, Faisal visits his grandfather's old house. One Friday, Grandfather says, let's clean the attic together.

Faisal and his cousin Noura climb the stairs. The attic is full of dusty boxes. Noura opens one small box. Inside, she finds an old folded map.

The map feels soft and brown, almost like cloth. It shows their house and a path. The path leads to a hill behind the house. Near the top of the hill, there is a mark shaped like an X.

What could this X mean? Faisal wonders. Grandfather studies the map carefully. My own father drew this map long ago, he explains. I believe he hid something near that hill.

The next morning, the cousins walk to the hill. They follow the map step by step. They pass three big rocks, just like the map shows. Then they see one old, twisted tree.

Near the tree, the cousins start to dig into the dirt. They dig for a while. Suddenly, Faisal feels something hard and metal. It is a small, rusty chest!

Inside the chest, they find an old compass, a faded photo, and a folded letter. The letter was written by their great-grandfather when he was a young boy.

Faisal and Noura carry the chest home. Grandfather's eyes grow wide with surprise. Then he tells them stories about his father as a child.

Faisal and his cousin Noura climbed the narrow, creaking stairs to the attic. It was a small, dim room, crowded with dusty old boxes stacked against the walls. Noura carefully opened one wooden box. Tucked inside, under some old cloth, she found a folded map.

The map felt soft and brown, almost like cloth instead of paper, and it crackled gently as she unfolded it. It showed their house and a trail leading toward a hill in the distance. Near the top of the hill, there was a small mark shaped like an X. It was their first real clue.

What could this clue mean, Faisal wondered, turning the old map over carefully in his hands. Grandfather studied it for a long, thoughtful moment. My own father drew this map long, long ago, he explained slowly. I believe he hid a family heirloom near that hill, though he never told me exactly what it was.

The next morning, eager to begin their small adventure, the cousins packed water bottles and a few snacks before setting out at sunrise, while the air was still cool. They followed the trail step by step, using the old map as their guide. They passed three big rocks, a clear landmark, just as the map showed. A little farther along the dry trail, they spotted one old, twisted tree standing alone, another landmark from the map.

Near the tree's roots, curious and excited, the cousins knelt down and began digging in the dry, stubborn dirt, taking turns with a small garden shovel they had brought along. They dug for a long time until Faisal's fingers struck something hard and metal buried beneath the surface. It was a small, rusty chest.

Inside, wrapped carefully in old cloth, they found an old compass, a faded photo of three smiling children, and a folded letter in careful handwriting. The letter, they realized with growing wonder, had been written by their curious great-grandfather when he was only a boy, decades before Grandfather was even born.

Thrilled beyond words, Faisal and Noura carried the heirloom chest home together, taking turns to hold it along the dusty trail. Grandfather's eyes widened with disbelief the moment he saw what his grandchildren had found. Then he happily told them story after story about his own father as a curious young boy growing up in that very same village.

versions.title: The Treasure Map
versions.text:
Every Friday afternoon, Faisal visited his grandfather's weathered old house at the edge of the village, and this particular Friday felt subtly, almost imperceptibly, different from all the rest, though he could not yet articulate exactly why. "Today," Grandfather announced, dusting off his hands with a mysterious smile, "let's finally clean out that attic together."

Faisal and his cousin Noura climbed the narrow, creaking stairs up to the attic, a small, dim room crowded with dusty old boxes stacked unevenly against every wall, their shapes barely discernible in the thin light filtering through one small, grimy window. Noura carefully opened one wooden box, and tucked inside, beneath a pile of faded cloth, she discovered a carefully folded, old map, its edges softened considerably by age and countless handlings.

The map felt brittle yet surprisingly pliable, almost like worn cloth rather than paper, and it crackled gently as she unfolded it across the dusty floorboards. It depicted their house clearly, along with a winding path leading away from it toward a distant hill. Near the summit of that hill, someone had drawn a small mark shaped like an X, right at the point where the path appeared to terminate entirely.

"What could this mysterious X possibly signify?" Faisal wondered aloud, turning the fragile map over carefully as dust drifted lazily through a beam of filtered sunlight, illuminating decades of accumulated dust.

Grandfather studied the old map for a long, thoughtful moment, his eyes narrowing with distant memory, as though some ancestor's voice were traveling backward through decades to reach him directly and urgently. "My own father drew this map long, long ago," he explained slowly, lowering himself onto an old wooden stool with a quiet, weary groan. "I have always believed he hid something important near that hill as a kind of keepsake, though he never once managed to decipher its full meaning for me before he passed away, taking the secret with him."

The next morning, eager to begin their small expedition, the cousins packed water bottles, a flashlight, and a few snacks into a canvas bag before setting out at sunrise, while the village still lay quiet and entirely undisturbed. They followed the map step by careful step, passing three enormous boulders arranged exactly as the old drawing showed, each one serving as a clear, unmistakable landmark along the winding trail. A little farther along the dusty path, they spotted one solitary, twisted tree standing at the edge of a sunbaked field, exactly as their great-grandfather had sketched it decades earlier, with the same crooked branches.

Near the tree's thick, tangled roots, curious and increasingly impatient, the cousins knelt down and began to excavate the dry, stubborn earth, taking turns with a small garden trowel they had deliberately brought along for precisely this purpose. They dug for what felt like a considerable stretch of time, their hands growing tired and coated in fine, clinging dust, until suddenly Faisal's fingers struck something hard and metallic buried just beneath the surface. It was a small, rusty metal chest, no larger than a shoebox, its corners worn smooth by decades spent buried underground, forgotten by everyone but the faded map itself.

Inside, carefully wrapped in old cloth, they discovered an old brass compass, a faded photograph of three smiling children standing on this very hill, and a folded, yellowed letter written in careful, looping handwriting. The letter, they soon realized with growing wonder, had been written and deliberately buried by their great-grandfather when he himself was only a boy, decades before Grandfather had even been born into the family line.

Thrilled beyond words, Faisal and Noura carried the heavy chest home together along the dusty, winding trail as the sun climbed steadily higher above the surrounding hills. Grandfather's eyes widened with pure disbelief the instant he recognized what his grandchildren had unearthed. Then, settling slowly into his favorite chair, he happily recounted story after story about his own father and ancestor as a curious, adventurous young boy growing up in that very village, long before any of them had ever been born, when the hills themselves looked much the same as they do today, patient and unchanging.

Climbing the narrow, creaking stairs, Faisal and his cousin Noura found themselves in a small, dim room crowded with dusty old boxes stacked unevenly against every wall, their shapes barely discernible in the thin light filtering through one small, grimy window. Beneath a pile of faded cloth inside one wooden box, Noura discovered a carefully folded, old map, its edges softened considerably by age and by countless anonymous handlings over the decades.

Brittle yet surprisingly pliable, the map crackled gently as she unfolded it across the dusty floorboards, revealing their house depicted clearly alongside a winding path leading toward a distant hill. Near the summit of that hill, someone had drawn a small mark shaped like an X, precisely at the point where the path appeared to terminate. "What could this mysterious X possibly signify?" Faisal wondered aloud, turning the fragile document over carefully as dust drifted lazily through a beam of filtered sunlight.

Grandfather studied the faded map for a long, thoughtful moment, his eyes narrowing with distant memory, as though some ancestor's voice were traveling backward through decades to reach him directly and insistently. "My own father drew this map long, long ago," he explained slowly, lowering himself onto an old wooden stool with a quiet, weary groan. "I have always believed he hid something important near that hill as a kind of keepsake, though he never once managed to decipher its full meaning for me before he passed away, taking whatever secret remained with him."

Eager to begin their small expedition the following morning, the cousins packed water bottles, a flashlight, and a few provisions into a canvas bag before setting out at sunrise, while the village still lay quiet and entirely undisturbed around them. Following the map step by deliberate step, they passed three enormous boulders arranged exactly as the old drawing indicated, each serving as an unmistakable landmark along the winding trail, until they eventually spotted one solitary, twisted tree standing at the edge of a sunbaked field, exactly as their great-grandfather had originally sketched it decades earlier.

Kneeling near the tree's thick, tangled roots, curious and increasingly impatient, the cousins began excavating the dry, stubborn earth, taking turns with a small garden trowel brought along for precisely this purpose. They dug for what felt like a considerable stretch of time, their hands growing tired and coated in fine, clinging dust, until suddenly Faisal's fingers struck something hard and metallic buried just beneath the surface: a small, rusty metal chest, no larger than a shoebox, its corners worn smooth by decades spent buried underground, forgotten by everyone but the faded map itself.

Carefully wrapped inside, they discovered an old brass compass, a faded photograph of three smiling children standing on this very hill generations earlier, and a folded, yellowed letter written in careful, looping handwriting. The letter, they realized with mounting wonder, had been composed and deliberately buried by their great-grandfather when he himself was merely a boy, decades before Grandfather had even been born into the family line that now stretched before them.

Thrilled beyond words, the two cousins carried the heavy chest home together along the dusty, winding trail as the sun climbed steadily higher above the surrounding hills. Grandfather's eyes widened with genuine disbelief the instant he recognized what his grandchildren had unearthed, and settling slowly into his favorite chair, he spent the remainder of that afternoon happily recounting story after story about his own father and ancestor as a curious, adventurous young boy growing up in that very village, long before any of them had ever been born, when the surrounding hills looked much the same as they do today, patient, unchanging, and quietly keeping their secrets.

Kneeling near the tree's thick, tangled roots, curious and increasingly impatient, the cousins began to excavate the dry, stubborn earth, taking turns with a small garden trowel brought along for precisely this purpose. They dug for what felt like a considerable stretch of time, their hands growing tired and coated in fine, clinging dust, until suddenly Faisal's fingers struck something hard and distinctly metallic buried just beneath the surface: a small, rusty metal chest, no larger than a shoebox, its corners worn smooth by decades spent buried underground, forgotten by everyone except the faded map itself.

Carefully wrapped inside, they discovered an old brass compass, a faded photograph of three smiling children standing on this very hill generations earlier, and a folded, yellowed letter composed in careful, looping handwriting. The letter, they realized with mounting wonder, had been written and deliberately buried by their great-grandfather when he himself was merely a boy, decades before Grandfather had even been born into the family line that now stretched unbroken before them.

Thrilled beyond words, the two cousins carried the heavy chest home together along the dusty, winding trail as the sun climbed steadily higher above the surrounding hills. Grandfather's eyes widened with genuine disbelief the instant he recognized precisely what his grandchildren had unearthed, and settling slowly into his favorite chair, he spent the remainder of that afternoon happily recounting story after story about his own father and ancestor as a curious, adventurous young boy growing up in that very village, long before any of them had ever been born, when the surrounding hills looked much the same as they do today: patient, unchanging, and quietly keeping their secrets for whoever might eventually come to unearth them.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says old family objects are more interesting than new things you can buy in a store. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the map, the chest, and Grandfather's reaction.

HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that old family objects are more interesting than new things from a store. The chest that Faisal and Noura excavated held a faded photograph, a compass, and a letter written by their own ancestor, which connected them directly to their great-grandfather's childhood. A new toy could never make Grandfather react the way he did, with such disbelief and joy, because a store-bought item carries no family history to decipher. Someone might argue that new things are more exciting because they work perfectly and have no damage, but the worn, faded condition of the chest's keepsakes is exactly what made them feel precious and irreplaceable.
